Passage – 1


The U.S. has allowed its waiver of sanctions on Iran's Chabahar port to lapse, indicating that India is now at a crossroads on how to
proceed with the port as a key connectivity initiative. Barring a belated waiver renewal, New Delhi must choose between accepting
sanctions and abandoning its $620 million investment, or proceeding with the project and risk strict U.S. sanctions.


India's "start-stop" engagement with Iran on developing a facility at the Shahid Beheshti terminal at Chabahar goes back decades, and
Prime Minister A.B. Vajpayee signed an MoU for the project in 2003. However, U.S. pressure on India to postpone plans aimed at stopping
Iran's nuclear programme led to construction delays. The Manmohan Singh government was unable to make much progress either, but
continued work on the Zaranj-Delaram highway to connect the Iran-Afghanistan border crossing to Kabul.


After the 2015 JCPOA, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government signed a trilateral agreement with Iran and Afghanistan to advance
trade and aid via Chabahar port and a highway into Afghanistan. Chabahar's importance grew as ties with Pakistan deteriorated and it
restricted India's transit access to Afghanistan. However, fate intervened again as U.S. President Donald Trump walked out of the JCPOA,
and began a "maximum pressure" campaign against Iran by re-implementing all sanctions.


While India was forced by the U.S. to give up Iranian oil imports and plans for the rail line, the U.S. built a "carve-out" for Chabahar, allowing
India to send wheat and medical supplies to Afghanistan. That carve-out is now at an end, with the Trump administration giving Delhi until
this month to "wind-down" its operations. Since November 2025, India has withdrawn personnel from Chabahar, prepaid its $120 million
investment commitment, and is considering transferring its stake in the Shahid Beheshti Terminal to an Iranian company.


The West Asia war has complicated the situation, and it is unclear when India will be able to re-engage with Iran or rebuild Chabahar.
Temporarily dropping the project may seem pragmatic. However, Chabahar is just one of several India's independent decisions that the
U.S. has thwarted, including demands to stop buying oil from Iran, Venezuela, and Russia. Giving in on Chabahar will not just end India's
connectivity plans with Iran, Central Asia and Afghanistan, but also damage its claims of sovereign autonomy and its ability to pursue an
independent foreign policy.


(387 words, Source: The Hindu)

Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 2


In the centuries after A.D. 1500, as European explorers became aware of the wide differences among the world's peoples in technology
and political organization, they assumed that those differences arose from differences in innate ability. With the rise of Darwinian theory,
explanations were recast in terms of natural selection and of evolutionary descent. Technologically primitive peoples were considered
evolutionary vestiges of human descent from apelike ancestors. The displacement of such peoples by colonists from industrialized
societies exemplified the survival of the fittest. With the later rise of genetics, the explanations were recast once again, in genetic terms.
Europeans became considered genetically more intelligent than Africans, and especially more so than Aboriginal Australians.


Today, segments of Western society publicly repudiate racism. Yet many Westerners continue to accept racist explanations privately or
subconsciously. Even educated white Americans, Europeans, and Australians, when the subject of Australian Aborigines comes up,
assume that there is something primitive about the Aborigines themselves. Many of the living descendants of those Aborigines who
survived the era of European colonization are now finding it difficult to succeed economically in white Australian society. A seemingly
compelling argument goes as follows. White immigrants to Australia built a literate, industrialized, politically centralized, democratic state
based on metal tools and on food production, all within a century of colonizing a continent where the Aborigines had been living as tribal
hunter-gatherers without metal for at least 40,000 years. Here were two successive experiments in human development, in which the

[[PAGE 3]]
environment was identical and the sole variable was the people occupying that environment.


The objection to such racist explanations is not just that they are loathsome, but also that they are wrong. Sound evidence for the
existence of human differences in intelligence that parallel human differences in technology is lacking. Peoples who until recently were
technologically primitive routinely master industrial technologies when given opportunities to do so.


An enormous effort by cognitive psychologists has gone into the search for differences in IQ between peoples of different geographic
origins now living in the same country. However, the peoples compared differ greatly in their social environment and educational
opportunities. Even our cognitive abilities as adults are heavily influenced by the social environment that we experienced during childhood.
Tests   of   cognitive   ability   tend   to   measure   cultural   learning   and   not   pure     innate   intelligence.   (384   words,   source:
https://newsroom.ucla.edu/)

The Mahabodhi Temple stands as one of the most revered and historically layered monuments in the Buddhist world, embodying both
spiritual awakening and architectural endurance. Located in Bodh Gaya, the site marks the exact spot where Siddhartha Gautama attained
enlightenment nearly 2,500 years ago. According to tradition, the young seeker meditated under a peepal tree for three days, culminating
in a moment of profound realization that transformed him into the Buddha, or the "Enlightened One."


Recognizing the sanctity of this event, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka commissioned the first shrine at this location in the 3rd century BCE,
making it one of the earliest formal Buddhist monuments. Over time, however, the structure underwent several transformations. The
present temple, with its soaring pyramidal tower rising approximately 55 metres, largely dates to the Gupta period (5th-6th century CE), a
time often associated with artistic and architectural refinement in the Indian subcontinent.


Beyond its historical origins, the temple complex is rich in symbolic elements. Adjacent to the shrine stands a descendant of the original
Bodhi Tree, under which the Buddha meditated. At its base lies the Vajrasana, or "Diamond Throne," believed to mark the precise spot of
enlightenment. The temple itself is enclosed by intricately carved stone railings, some dating back to the 2nd century BCE, depicting
motifs from Buddhist lore and everyday life.


Yet, the journey of the Mahabodhi Temple has not been uninterrupted. With the decline of Buddhism in India after the 8th century, the site
gradually fell into neglect and even changed custodial hands. By the late 19th century, it required significant restoration, which was
undertaken with the involvement of both Burmese patrons and British officials. A prolonged legal and religious struggle eventually restored
its status as a Buddhist shrine, though its management continues to reflect a shared religious legacy.


Today, the Mahabodhi Temple is not merely an architectural relic but a living centre of pilgrimage, drawing devotees from across the globe.

centuries of devotion, conflict, and renewal.

The rise of the Indian Writing in English is, at the onset, to be located historically. The first connection that we should be looking at is the
introduction of the English language as a medium of instruction in India and the introduction of English literature as a subject in the
Universities. Macaulay's Minute introduced in 1833 provided for the introduction of English as a medium of instruction with the claim that
"the English tongue would be the most useful for our native subjects." While presenting his famous minute, Macaulay admitted quite
candidly that he had not read any of the Sanskrit and Arabic books and yet did not desist from making such a pronouncement: "…A single
shelf of a good European library is worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia. …All the historical information which has been
collected in the Sanskrit language is less than what may be found in the paltry abridgements used at preparatory schools of England…"

[[PAGE 6]]
India, thus became a kind of testing ground for the launch of English literature in the classroom at a time when English Universities were
still steeped in the Latin and Greek classics. English was, as a result, introduced in educational institutions, Courts and offices thus
dislodging the traditional use of Arabic and Sanskrit as a mode of communication and documentation. Lord William Bentick announced in
1835 that the government would "favour English Language alone" henceforth and would move towards "a knowledge of English literature
and Science through the medium of English language alone." The Wood Dispatch of 1854 proclaimed the establishment of the Universities
at Bombay, Madras and Calcutta and thereafter made the English language accessible to students, professors and also the officials of
Government offices. To begin with the introduction of English at these levels had some interesting repercussions. What is pejoratively
called "Babu English" today became the first offspring of the unholy encounter between the British English language and the unwilling
Babu. The 'art and craft' and discomfort with which they used the language in the offices in course became a matter of derision. In the
arena of literary studies too English began to assert itself.

capacities are stretched. India's humanitarian aid and disaster relief to our partner countries is focused on providing timely assistance to
save lives, alleviate suffering, maintain and protect human dignity during and post disaster. The Indian Army undertakes the deployment of
troops for rescue and relief, establishment of field hospitals, restoration of essential infrastructure, and delivery of humanitarian aid. The
Indian Navy plays a critical role through evacuation of Indian nationals from abroad, transportation of relief material, and deployment of
ships and helicopters for maritime and littoral assistance. The Indian Air Force provides strategic and tactical airlift by ferrying relief
supplies, medical teams, and disaster response personnel to affected areas, while also undertaking evacuation and rescue missions.
Complementing these efforts, the Indian Coast Guard assists during cyclones, tsunamis, earthquakes, oil platform fires, and flooding in
coastal regions, ensuring rapid response and maritime safety.

The Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters has awarded the 2026 Abel Prize to [1], director emeritus at the Max Planck Institute for
Mathematics in Bonn and professor emeritus at the University of Bonn, "for introducing powerful tools in arithmetic geometry and solving
long-standing diophantine conjectures by Mordell and Lang." In its citation, the prize committee honours [1] as "a towering figure in
arithmetic geometry. His ideas and results have reshaped the field, settling major long-standing conjectures, while also establishing new
frameworks that have guided decades of subsequent work. His exceptional achievements unite geometric and arithmetic perspectives

[[PAGE 10]]
and exemplify the power of deep structural insight." In 1983, [1] became famous overnight in the mathematical community when he
surprisingly proved Mordell's conjecture using entirely novel methods. The idea behind Mordell's conjecture is thousands of years old.
Already the ancient Greek mathematician Diophantus of Alexandria wanted to find out how many integer solutions an equation such as a²
+ b² = c² has. Because of the Pythagorean theorem, this corresponds to the practical question of how many right-angled triangles with
integer side lengths there are. It is now clear: There are infinitely many of them.

The anti-defection framework in India is governed by the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution of India, introduced through the 52nd
Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 and later strengthened by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003. Its primary objective is to
ensure stability in governance by discouraging opportunistic political defections.


A legislator may incur disqualification if they voluntarily give up the membership of their political party, or if they vote or abstain from
voting contrary to the party whip without prior permission. The expression "voluntarily giving up membership" has been interpreted broadly
and is not confined to formal resignation; it may be inferred from conduct, public declarations, or alignment with rival political formations.


Independent legislators are disqualified if they join any political party after election. Nominated members may join a political party within
six months of taking their seat, failing which they lose that flexibility. The law no longer recognizes "split" as a valid defense. Only a merger
is recognized, and that too when at least two-thirds of the members of a legislative party agree to such merger. Members who do not
accept the merger are not deemed to have defected and may continue separately.


The authority to decide disqualification petitions lies with the Speaker or Chairman of the House. Although originally intended to be final,
the Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu clarified that such decisions are subject to judicial review on limited grounds such as
mala fide intent, violation of constitutional mandates, or perversity.

Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, contingent contracts are governed by Sections 31 to 36. A contingent contract is a contract to do or
not do something depending on the happening or non-happening of an uncertain future event, which must be collateral to the contract.
The event should not form part of the reciprocal promises themselves but must be an independent condition upon which performance

depends on the happening of an event, it cannot be enforced until the event occurs. If the event becomes impossible, the contract
becomes void. Importantly, the impossibility must relate to the specific event contemplated by the parties, and not merely a similar or
alternative occurrence. In cases where the contract depends on the non-happening of an event within a fixed time, the contract becomes
enforceable when the time expires and the event has not occurred. However, if before the expiry of the specified time, the event becomes
impossible, the contract becomes enforceable immediately, as the condition of non-happening is conclusively satisfied.


Conversely, where the contract depends on the happening of an event within a fixed time, and such event becomes impossible before the
expiry of that time, the contract becomes void immediately. Thus, the law distinguishes carefully between (i) contracts dependent on
happening, (ii) contracts dependent on non-happening, and (iii) contracts tied to a specific time frame. A crucial principle is that the event
must be construed strictly as agreed between the parties. If the contract specifies the occurrence of a particular event in a particular
manner (for example, destruction by fire), the occurrence of a similar result by a different cause (such as demolition) will not satisfy the
condition.

examine the substance of the transaction, particularly whether the uncertain event is merely collateral to a genuine transaction or
constitutes the sole basis of the agreement.

With the rapid growth of digital commerce, contracts formed through electronic means commonly known as e-contracts have gained legal
recognition under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Indian Contract Act, 1872. An e-contract is formed through electronic
communication, such as emails, clicks, or digital acceptance mechanisms, provided that the essential elements of a valid contract i.e.,
offer, acceptance, lawful consideration, and free consent are satisfied.


Click-wrap agreements, where users explicitly click "I agree," are generally enforceable as they demonstrate clear consent. Browse-wrap
agreements, where terms are merely posted on a website without requiring explicit acceptance, are enforceable only when the user has
actual or constructive knowledge of the terms. Courts often scrutinize whether reasonable notice of such terms was provided. The validity
of e-contracts also depends on proper communication of offer and acceptance. The "click" or electronic assent must be free, informed,
and not induced by misrepresentation, coercion, or fraud. Where terms are hidden, misleading, or presented in a manner that a reasonable
user would not notice, consent may be vitiated.


Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, consumers engaging in e-commerce transactions are entitled to protection against unfair trade
practices, misleading advertisements, and defective goods or deficient services. E-commerce platforms may be classified either as
intermediaries (facilitating transactions) or as sellers, depending on the degree of control exercised over the transaction. Liability often
turns on this distinction. The Act recognizes rights such as the right to be informed, the right to seek redressal, and protection against
unfair contracts. In digital transactions, obvious pricing errors or technical glitches (such as a product being listed at an unrealistically low
price due to system error) may affect the validity of consent. Where a reasonable user would recognize the error, such apparent
acceptance may not amount to genuine and informed consent. An unfair contract may include terms that are excessively one-sided, such
as unilateral modification clauses, disproportionate penalties, or exclusion of liability for negligence. Additionally, digital transactions often
raise issues regarding jurisdiction and standard form contracts. Courts may examine whether consumers had a meaningful opportunity to
understand terms, whether the platform exercised dominance, and whether contractual clauses unfairly restrict consumer remedies. Thus,
while e-contracts are valid, their enforceability is closely tied to transparency, fairness, and genuine consent, especially in consumer
transactions.

Under the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the right of private defence is recognised as a natural right allowing individuals to protect their body
and property against unlawful aggression. Sections 96 to 106 provide that an act done in the exercise of this right is not an offence,
provided it falls within prescribed limits.


The right arises when there is a reasonable apprehension of danger to body or property. It is not necessary that the offence be actually
committed; the apprehension itself must be real and immediate. However, the right is preventive and not punitive-it cannot be exercised as
retaliation after the danger has ceased. The extent of this right depends on the nature of the threat. In certain circumstances, the right
extends to causing death, particularly where the assault reasonably causes apprehension of death, grievous hurt, rape, kidnapping, or
wrongful confinement. However, the force used must be proportionate to the threat perceived.


The law imposes clear limitations. The right cannot be exercised against acts done by public servants acting in good faith under colour of
office, unless there is reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt. Further, the right does not extend to situations where there is
sufficient time to seek protection from public authorities.Another important limitation is that the harm caused in private defence must not
be more than necessary. If the defender exceeds this limit, the protection is lost, and criminal liability may arise depending on the intention
and circumstances. In assessing such cases, courts examine whether the accused acted in good faith, whether the apprehension was
reasonable, and whether the response was proportionate. The law thus balances the need for self-preservation with the broader objective
of preventing misuse of defensive rights.

difficult situations such as world wars and major disasters. That stoicism and sense of "accepting what can't be changed" seems to be

political, and cultural life --- and indeed our own biological substrate --- that stoic acceptance might not be the way to go.

In the years before Lehman Brothers went bust in 2008, plunging the world into financial crisis, macroeconomists were understandably
worried. But they worried about the wrong thing: not over-indebted American banks, but over-thrifty Asian economies. According to this
theory, Asia's determination to accumulate dollar reserves was depressing interest rates, tempting Americans to overspend. The upshot
was that Asia earned more than it spent, resulting in large trade surpluses. This enabled America to spend more than it earned, reflected in
a yawning current-account deficit.


These "global imbalances" are back. The new imbalances are not quite as big as those of two decades ago. The world's deficit countries
had a combined current-account gap of 1.6% of global GDP in 2025, compared with a peak of 2.6% in 2006. President Donald Trump cited
America's deficit to justify his "Liberation Day" tariffs last year. President Emmanuel Macron of France called China's surpluses
"unbearable" on his visit to Beijing in December.


One answer is America's budget deficit. Tax cuts or higher welfare spending increase American consumption and reduce saving. That can
lift interest rates and thus the dollar-which makes exports less competitive, deepening the trade deficit.

[[PAGE 24]]
Other commentators are equally confident that the culprit is once again Asia, especially China. China subsidises its manufacturers,
resulting in excess capacity. What these firms cannot sell at home, they dump abroad. This crowds out local manufacturers, destroying
jobs and obliging countries like America to increase their fiscal deficits to restore demand and curb unemployment.


What has suppressed domestic spending in China is a property slump. If China is the culprit for imbalances, it has perpetrated more a
blunder than a crime. Its big fiscal deficits are a political choice not an economic necessity.


The causes of global imbalances are not, then, as clear as some commentators allege. All of the suspects are implicated. But the ending
could still be bad.

In her essay "The Gentle Leviathan", Niraja Gopal Jayal argues that by separating the non-justiciable welfare commitments from the
enforceable "liberty rights" of Part III, the Constitution grounded welfare in a language of state responsibility tempered by discretion. "The
Indian state adheres to a needs-based conception of justice in theory," she observes, "but in practice follows a philosophy of welfare
manifestly based in ideas of charity and benevolence. The idea of a right to welfare is clearly precluded".


Income transfers and subsidies, therefore, are not sudden political inventions; they are contemporary instruments through which an older
constitutional commitment to social and economic justice is expressed.


There are, however, important differences between welfare in its classical sense-echoed in the Constitution-and what is today described
as the "new" welfare associated with freebies. In its classical conception, welfare was understood as structurally integral to liberal
capitalism. John Maynard Keynes anticipated that public and private investment could sustain a high and stable level of employment,
wages, and effective demand. If profits were reinvested rather than hoarded, growth would expand the economic pie in ways that
supported both accumulation and social provisioning.


Early experiments in India partly moved in this direction. In Tamil Nadu, K. Kamaraj expanded free education and school meals from the
late 1950s. The promise of heavily subsidised rice by C.N. Annadurai in 1967 marked a decisive shift: welfare became not only
developmental policy but also a visible political claim.


Around the same time, Kerala moved towards near-universal schooling through extensive public provisioning and regulation of aided
schools well before education was recognised nationally as a fundamental right. Maharashtra's Employment Guarantee Scheme of the
early 1970s, conceived partly to provide rural employment and slow distress migration to Bombay, offered another example of welfare tied
directly to the creation of work rather than simple transfers, anticipating later national programmes such as the MGNREGA (Echeverri-Gent
1988). In these early initiatives, welfare was tied to the expansion of capabilities and public services, reinforcing attempts to steer
capitalism in a more humane direction.


If classical welfare sought to integrate citizens into the productive economy as rights-bearing members, the "new" welfare operates
through the idiom of beneficiaries or labharthis dependent on the benefactor's largesse. Entitlements grounded in universal rights and
systematic public provisioning give way to targeted distributions of private goods such as cycles, laptops, televisions, or cash transfers.
Enabled by digital identification and direct bank credits, welfare can now be finely individuated even when directed at specific classes or
communities.
